name: The Hackberry of Fuente del Portillon

location.address: Fuente del Portillon, road from Pampaneira to Portugos, Granada

pin_evidence: Register coordinate only (the Junta's hydrological-plan appendix lists the same tree in UTM 467406.94 / 4088154.75, the same register family). No photograph or GPS observation of the trunk found. iNaturalist has nothing on a nettle tree here.

official_register.name: Arboles y arboledas singulares de Andalucia (REDIAM)

access: Free. Public land beside the Pampaneira to Portugos road, near the Fuente del Portillon spring; seen from the road.
transport: On the road from Pampaneira to Portugos, a few km from Pampaneira (estimated from the map); Pampaneira has a bus from Granada.
alive_evidence: None dated. Register sheet only (date of the sheet not stated).
facts: Sheet: total height 25.0 m, trunk 3.0 m to first fork, girth 4.75 m at 1.30 m and 8.30 m at the base, crown 19.0 by 20.5 m (projection 305.91 sq m). Source: sheet PDF.
Sheet: listed for size, great height and a notable trunk that looks like two stems fused into one over time. Source: sheet PDF.
Sheet: the trunk is half covered by a web of ivy that climbs to high levels; the trunk forks into two main limbs that keep dividing into an oval crown that casts huge shade. Source: sheet PDF.

Sheet, setting: beside the Pampaneira to Portugos road, very close to the Fuente del Portillon, with other nettle trees, on sandy gently sloping ground in a ravine landscape where iron-rich (ferruginous) spring water is common. Source: sheet PDF.
verify_notes: Register only (the appendix is the same authority). No vitality evidence, no photograph, no pin evidence: single official source, flagged 'register only'. Does not meet the findable gate until a photo or confirmed pin turns up. Species Celtis australis stated by the sheet.
story:
At the base this hackberry measures 8.30 metres round, and its trunk looks like two stems that fused into one over the years. The Junta de Andalucia's register listed it for that trunk, for its size and for its height of 25 metres. At chest height the girth is 4.75 metres.

Three metres up, the trunk forks into two main limbs that keep dividing into an oval crown about 20 metres across, which the sheet says casts huge shade. Ivy has spread over half the trunk in a web that climbs high into the tree.

It grows beside the road between Pampaneira and Portugos in the Alpujarra, very close to the spring called the Fuente del Portillon, with other hackberries around it on sandy, gently sloping ground. This is ravine country, and the sheet notes that iron-rich spring water is common here. The land is public and the tree can be seen from the road.

Two things are missing. The register is the only source we have found for this tree, and no dated photograph of it has been published, so the pin is the register's point rather than a fix taken at the trunk. Nobody has published an age either. If you drive this road and find it, or know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, half covered in ivy and 8.30 metres round at the base, forking at 3 metres into two limbs. It stands beside the Pampaneira to Portugos road, near the Fuente del Portillon.

name: The Roadside Oak of Las Balsas

location.address: Las Balsas, mountain road between Busquistar and Trevelez / Capileira, Sierra Nevada, Granada

pin_evidence: Register coordinate only (the Junta's hydrological-plan appendix lists it in UTM 475113.06 / 4091648.50, same authority). No photo or GPS observation found; the only iNaturalist point within 150 m is an unrelated plant.

official_register.name: Arboles y arboledas singulares de Andalucia (REDIAM)

access: Free to see from public land at the road edge in Sierra Nevada Natural Park; look from a safe pull-off, not the carriageway.
transport: On the mountain road between Busquistar and Trevelez; best reached by car.
facts: Sheet: total height 19.0 m, short trunk 0.5 m, girth 4.05 m at 0.45 m height (not at 1.30 m, because the trunk forks low) and 4.40 m at the base, crown 25.5 by 21.2 m (projection 424.59 sq m). Source: sheet PDF.

Sheet: listed for great size; a short trunk with a tremendous fork carrying powerful main limbs arranged like counterweights, forming an irregular crown that covers part of the road. Source: sheet PDF.
Sheet: it does not go unnoticed by any driver on the mountain road to Trevelez from Busquistar. Source: sheet PDF.
Sheet, setting: on the edge of a slope, among sweet chestnuts and sparse broom (Genista cinerea), light north-east slope. Source: sheet PDF.
verify_notes: Register only, no photo, no pin evidence, no vitality evidence. Girth measured at 0.45 m. The appendix lists it without species; species Quercus pyrenaica is from the sheet's label. Delivered flagged; cannot ship until a photograph or confirmed pin exists.
story:
The Junta de Andalucia's register says no driver on the mountain road from Busquistar to Trevelez fails to notice this oak, and that is not a figure of speech. Its crown spreads about 25 metres and covers part of the road.

The trunk is barely a trunk. Half a metre above the ground it splits in a tremendous fork, and the powerful main limbs that come out of it are arranged, in the sheet's words, like counterweights, balancing an irregular crown over the slope on one side and the tarmac on the other. Because it forks so low, the register measured its girth 45 centimetres above the ground instead of the usual 1.30 metres, and found 4.05 metres there and 4.40 at the base. It is 19 metres tall.

It is a Pyrenean oak, growing on the edge of a slope among sweet chestnuts and sparse broom at a place called Las Balsas, inside the Sierra Nevada Natural Park. The sheet names the road both as Busquistar to Trevelez and as Capileira to Trevelez.

The register is the only source for this tree, and no dated photograph of it has been published. Nobody has published an age. Pull off where it is safe to look rather than stopping on the carriageway, and if you know its history, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown hanging over part of the road, carried on huge limbs that fork only half a metre above the ground. It stands on the slope edge at Las Balsas, among sweet chestnuts.
